title: The Lebesgue integral
objectives: Build expectation as a Lebesgue integral from simple functions.

screens.title: Slicing the range
screens.prose: Topic 3.2 is optional: it serves desk quant and derivatives pricing roles. Pick $U$ uniformly from $[0, 1]$ and let $X = U^2$. We cut the values into bands of height $\tfrac12$: $\varphi_1 = \lfloor 2X \rfloor / 2$, which is $\tfrac12$ where $U \ge 0.707$.
screens.question: What is $E[\varphi_1]$? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: The function $\varphi_1$ takes two values. Weight each by its chance.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply each value of $\varphi_1$ by the chance that it takes it.

byKey.level: You gave the top value $\tfrac12$. It happens only on part of the interval, so weight it by its chance.
byKey.chance: You gave $P(U \ge 0.707)$. Multiply it by the value $\tfrac12$ the function takes there.
byKey.third: You gave the exact mean of $U^2$. The two-band function sits below $X$, so its mean is smaller.

explain.text: $\varphi_1$ equals $\tfrac12$ exactly when $2U^2 \ge 1$, that is $U \ge 1/\sqrt2$. That has chance $1 - 0.7071 = 0.2929$, so $E[\varphi_1] = \tfrac12 \times 0.2929 = 0.1464$.

screens.title: More bands
screens.prose: Slide $n$. Each $\varphi_n$ has $2^n$ bands of height $2^{-n}$ and never rises above $X$. The caption gives $E[\varphi_n]$ exactly.
screens.question: What number does $E[\varphi_n]$ rise towards? Give 4 decimal places.

widget.accept: $\tfrac13$: the gap to it roughly halves with each step
widget.label: Limit

hints.text: Watch the gap between the caption and $0.3333$ as $n$ grows.
Each gap is about half the one before, so the means close in on $\tfrac13 = E[U^2]$.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac13$. The bands hug $X$ more closely at every step, and the means rise to its mean.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at where the caption values are heading, not where they are now.

byKey.read: That is $E[\varphi_6]$. The means keep rising with $n$.
byKey.half: You gave the largest value of $X$ halved. The means settle well below that.

explain.text: $E[\varphi_n]$ is 0.1464, 0.2317, 0.2794, 0.3052, 0.3188, 0.3259 for $n = 1$ to 6. The shortfall from $\tfrac13$ halves each time, so the limit is $\tfrac13 = \int_0^1 u^2\,du$.

screens.title: Simple functions and the integral
screens.prose: A **simple function** takes finitely many values: $\varphi = \sum_k a_k \mathbf{1}_{A_k}$, with $E[\varphi] = \sum_k a_k P(A_k)$. For $X \ge 0$ the **Lebesgue integral** is $E[X] = \sup\{E[\varphi] : 0 \le \varphi \le X,\ \varphi \text{ simple}\}$. In general $E[X] = E[X^+] - E[X^-]$, unless both are infinite.
screens.question: Our $\varphi_n$ are simple. Over which functions does the supremum run?

options.text: Simple functions that lie below $X$.
Strips of the domain $[0, 1]$, as in a Riemann sum.
options.why: You described a Riemann sum, which cuts the domain. The Lebesgue integral cuts the range into bands.

options.text: Simple functions that lie above $X$.
options.why: You took upper approximations. The supremum needs functions below $X$, which push the integral up from underneath.

options.text: Every function below $X$.
options.why: You included functions with no integral yet. Only simple functions have an integral by definition, so the supremum runs over those.

hints.text: Look at where each $\varphi_n$ sits relative to the curve.
Every $\varphi_n$ lies on or below $X$.
The definition takes the best simple function from below.

feedback.correct: The supremum of $E[\varphi]$ over simple $\varphi \le X$. The $\varphi_n$ are a sequence that reaches it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The integral is built from simple functions that stay under $X$.

explain.text: A simple function has a finite sum for its integral. $E[X]$ is the best value reachable from below, and $\varphi_n$ gets there for $X = U^2$.

screens.title: A payoff is simple
screens.prose: A bet pays £0, £5 or £20 with chances 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2. It takes three values, so it is simple.
screens.question: What is its expected payoff, in £?

hints.text: Multiply each value by its chance, then add.
The three terms are 0, 1.5 and 4.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each payoff by its chance.

byKey.avg: You averaged the three payoffs and ignored the chances.
byKey.sum: You added the payoffs. Each one counts only with its chance.
byKey.swap: You paired the chances with the wrong payoffs: 0.2 with £5 and 0.3 with £20. Match £5 with 0.3 and £20 with 0.2.

explain.text: The sum is $0 \times 0.5 + 5 \times 0.3 + 20 \times 0.2 = 5.5$. Each value is weighted by the chance of its set.

screens.title: Edge case: zero except on a null set
screens.prose: The Dirichlet function $\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}$ is 1 on the rationals and 0 elsewhere in $[0, 1]$. Its Riemann sums never agree: every lower sum is 0 and every upper sum is 1. So it has no Riemann integral. Under a uniform $U$ the rationals have chance 0 (level 1).
screens.question: What is $E[\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}(U)]$?

options.text: 0, because it is simple and $1 \cdot P(\mathbb{Q}) + 0 \cdot P(\mathbb{Q}^c) = 0$.
1, because the rationals are dense in $[0, 1]$, so every window has one.
options.why: You counted density as size. The rationals are dense but countable, so their chance is 0.

options.text: $\tfrac12$, halfway between the lower and upper Riemann sums, 0 and 1.
options.why: You averaged two Riemann sums that never meet. The Lebesgue integral weights values by chance.

options.text: It does not exist, as for the Riemann integral of this function.
options.why: You carried the Riemann failure over. Every simple function has an integral.

hints.text: Write the function as $1 \cdot \mathbf{1}_A + 0 \cdot \mathbf{1}_{A^c}$ with $A = \mathbb{Q}$.
The only value with weight is 1, and its set is $\mathbb{Q}$.
$P(\mathbb{Q}) = 0$ by level 1, so the sum is 0.

feedback.correct: 0. A variable that is 0 except on a null set has integral 0. So variables equal almost surely have equal means.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the chance of each value's set, not the size of the set.

byKey.b: Dense does not mean large. The rationals have chance 0.
byKey.c: The two Riemann sums are 0 and 1. The integral uses chances instead.

explain.text: $\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}$ is simple, so $E = 1 \cdot P(\mathbb{Q}) = 0$. Changing a variable on a null set never changes its mean.

screens.title: The layer-cake formula
screens.prose: For $X \ge 0$, $E[X] = \int_0^\infty P(X > t)\,dt$: the range is cut into layers, and each layer counts its chance. For $X = U^2$, $P(X > t) = P(U > \sqrt t) = 1 - \sqrt t$ on $[0, 1]$.
screens.question: What is the area under the curve? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: Integrate $1$ and $\sqrt t$ separately from 0 to 1.
$\int_0^1 \sqrt t\,dt = \tfrac23$.
$1 - \tfrac23 = \tfrac13$.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac13$, the same value the bands $\varphi_n$ reached from below.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the area under $\sqrt t$ from the unit square.

byKey.tri: You treated the curve as a straight line from 1 to 0. It is bent, so the area is smaller.
byKey.rootarea: You found the area under $\sqrt t$. The curve is $1 - \sqrt t$.

explain.text: $\int_0^1 (1 - \sqrt t)\,dt = 1 - \tfrac23 = \tfrac13$. Slicing the range into layers gives the same mean as slicing it into bands.

screens.title: A payout with no ceiling
screens.prose: A game pays $X = 2^K$, where $K$ is the number of tosses up to the first head, so $P(K = k) = 2^{-k}$. We cap the payout at $2^m$. The bars show the capped mean for $m = 1$ to 5.
screens.question: What is $E[\min(X, 2^m)]$ for $m = 10$?

widget.accept: $m + 1 = 11$: ten terms equal to 1, plus $2^{10} \cdot P(K > 10) = 1$
widget.label: Capped mean

hints.text: Each toss count $k \le m$ adds $2^k \cdot 2^{-k}$.
That is 1 per term. Past $m$, the payout is capped at $2^m$ with chance $2^{-m}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add one term for each $k \le m$, then the capped tail.

byKey.terms: You counted the ten terms and left out the capped tail. It adds $2^{10} \times 2^{-10} = 1$.
byKey.cap: You gave the cap itself. The chance of reaching it is only $2^{-10}$.

explain.text: Each $k \le m$ contributes $2^k \cdot 2^{-k} = 1$, and the cap adds $2^m P(K > m) = 1$. So the capped mean is $m + 1$, which has no upper bound as $m$ grows.

screens.title: Does every random variable have a mean?
screens.prose: The capped means $m + 1$ keep growing. A colleague says the chances $2^{-k}$ shrink fast, so $E[X]$ must be a finite number.
screens.question: What is $E[X]$ for the full game?

options.text: $\infty$: the capped means rise without bound.
Finite, because the chances $2^{-k}$ shrink.
options.why: You trusted the shrinking chances. The payouts $2^k$ grow just as fast, so every term is 1.

options.text: Undefined: no mean exists.
options.why: You treated an infinite mean as missing. For $X \ge 0$ the integral is always defined, possibly $\infty$.

options.text: 11, the value at $m = 10$.
options.why: You stopped at one cap. The integral is the supremum over all caps.

hints.text: Ask what the supremum of $m + 1$ over all $m$ is.
The sequence $m + 1$ has no upper bound.
$E[X] = \sup_m (m + 1) = \infty$.

feedback.correct: $\infty$. Every $X \ge 0$ has a mean in $[0, \infty]$, and this one is infinite.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The mean is the supremum of the capped means.

byKey.b: The terms are all 1, so shrinking chances alone do not help.
byKey.c: A non-negative variable always has an integral, possibly infinite.

explain.text: $E[X] = \sup_m E[\min(X, 2^m)] = \sup_m (m + 1) = \infty$. A non-negative variable always has a mean, but it may be infinite.

screens.title: Monotonicity passes to the supremum
screens.prose: For simple functions, $\varphi \le \psi$ gives $E[\varphi] \le E[\psi]$ by finite arithmetic. We want $X \le Y$ to give $E[X] \le E[Y]$.
screens.question: Why does $X \le Y$ imply $E[X] \le E[Y]$?

options.text: Every simple $\varphi \le X$ is also $\le Y$, so $E[Y]$ takes a supremum over a larger set.
At each outcome $X(\omega) \le Y(\omega)$, and the integral adds up the outcomes.
options.why: You summed over outcomes. There are uncountably many, and the integral is not a sum over points.

options.text: Because $P$ is monotone on events.
options.why: You used monotonicity of $P$. It is the starting point for simple functions, but $X$ and $Y$ need the supremum argument.

options.text: It holds only when $X$ and $Y$ are simple.
options.why: You limited it to simple functions. The supremum carries it to every non-negative variable.

hints.text: Compare the two sets of simple functions the suprema run over.
A simple function below $X$ is also below $Y$.
A supremum over a larger set cannot be smaller.

feedback.correct: The set for $E[Y]$ contains the set for $E[X]$. Linearity passes to the limit in the same way, using level sets.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two families of simple functions.

explain.text: If $\varphi \le X \le Y$, then $\varphi$ is a simple function below $Y$ too. So the supremum for $Y$ is over at least as many functions, and $E[X] \le E[Y]$.

screens.title: The integral in code
screens.prose: Write `dyadic_mean(n)`, the mean of $\varphi_n$ for $X = U^2$: band $k$ is $\tfrac{k}{2^n}$ with chance $\sqrt{(k+1)/2^n} - \sqrt{k/2^n}$. Then write `simple_mean(values, probs)`, the exact mean of a simple function, with `Fraction`s.
screens.question: Complete both functions.

widget.prelude:
from fractions import Fraction
import math

hints.text: Band $k$ has value $k/2^n$ and chance $\sqrt{(k+1)/N} - \sqrt{k/N}$ with $N = 2^n$.
Sum the value times the chance over $k$ from 0 to $N - 1$.
`simple_mean` is `sum(a * p ...)` with a start value of `Fraction(0)`.

feedback.correct: Right. The simple means rise to $\tfrac13$, and the gap roughly halves each step.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each band's value by the chance of its band.

explain.text: `dyadic_mean` is the simple-function sum $\sum_k a_k P(A_k)$ for the band sets. The gap to $\tfrac13$ is 0.0540 at $n = 3$ and 0.0074 at $n = 6$.

screens.title: A tranche loss
screens.prose: A credit portfolio's loss $L$ is exponential with mean £10m, so $P(L > t) = e^{-t/10}$. A senior tranche pays out the loss above £20m: $(L - 20)^+ = \int_{20}^\infty \mathbf{1}_{\{L > t\}}\,dt$.
screens.question: What is the tranche's expected loss, $E[(L - 20)^+]$, in £m? Give 4 decimal places, the number only.

hints.text: Integrate the tail chance from 20 upwards.

feedback.correct: £1.3534m. The layer-cake formula turns a payoff above a strike into an area under the tail.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate $P(L > t)$ from $t = 20$ to infinity.

byKey.mean: You gave the mean loss of the whole portfolio. The tranche pays only above £20m.
byKey.noscale: You gave $e^{-2}$, the chance of passing £20m. Multiply by the scale 10.
byKey.twenty: You multiplied by 20. The area under $e^{-t/10}$ from 20 has scale 10.

explain.text: $E[(L-20)^+] = \int_{20}^\infty P(L > t)\,dt = 10e^{-2} = 1.3534$. Desks price tranches this way: the expected loss is the area under the tail beyond the attachment point.

ideas: A simple function has $E[\varphi] = \sum_k a_k P(A_k)$. For $X \ge 0$, $E[X]$ is the supremum of $E[\varphi]$ over simple $\varphi \le X$.
The integral slices the range, not the domain. A function that is 0 except on a null set has integral 0.
A non-negative variable always has a mean, possibly $\infty$, and $E[X] = \int_0^\infty P(X > t)\,dt$.

formula.name: Layer-cake formula
formula.note: Further reading: Williams, Probability with Martingales, chapter 5, and Shreve II, section 1.4.

summary.trap: Shrinking chances do not guarantee a finite mean: the payout can grow as fast.

quiz.prose: A loss $X \ge 0$ has $P(X > t) = (1 + t)^{-3}$ for $t \ge 0$.
quiz.question: What is $E[X]$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate the tail chance from 0 to infinity.

quiz.prose: A payout $X \ge 0$ has $P(X > t) = \dfrac{1}{1 + t}$ for $t \ge 0$.
quiz.question: What is $E[X]$?

options.text: $\infty$, because $\int_0^\infty \tfrac{dt}{1 + t}$ diverges.
1, because the tail chance starts at 1 and then falls.
options.why: You read off the value of the tail at $t = 0$. The mean is the area under the tail.

options.text: $\tfrac12$, because the tail has halved by $t = 1$, so the mean is a half.
options.why: You used one point of the curve. The area needs the whole tail, and it is not finite.

options.text: It has no mean, because the tail never reaches 0.
options.why: You treated infinity as missing. A non-negative variable has mean $\infty$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate the tail chance over all $t \ge 0$.

explain.text: The tail $\tfrac{1}{1 + t}$ falls too slowly: its integral is $\ln(1 + t)$, which grows without bound.

quiz.prose: $Y = X$ except on an event of chance 0, and $E[X] = 3$.
quiz.question: What is $E[Y]$?

widget.accept: 3: variables equal almost surely have equal means
widget.label: $E[Y]$

feedback.correct: 3. A null set contributes nothing to an integral.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A set of chance 0 cannot change a mean.

byKey.zero: You treated the changed outcomes as if they cancelled everything. They have chance 0, so they change nothing.

explain.text: $Y - X$ is 0 except on a null set, so $E[Y - X] = 0$ and $E[Y] = E[X] = 3$.
